units.title: 1 Characteristics and classification of living organisms

outcomes.text: Describe movement as an action causing a change of position or place.
Describe respiration as the cell reactions that break down nutrients and release energy.
Describe sensitivity as detecting and responding to changes.
Describe growth as a permanent increase in size and dry mass.
Describe reproduction as making more of the same kind of organism.
Describe excretion as removing metabolic waste and excess substances.
Describe nutrition as taking in materials for energy, growth and development.

topics.title: 1.2 Concept and uses of classification systems

outcomes.text: State that organisms are classified into groups by shared features.
Describe a species as organisms that reproduce to give fertile offspring.
Describe the binomial system: genus and species names.
Construct and use dichotomous keys.
Explain that classification systems aim to reflect evolutionary relationships.
Explain that DNA base sequences are used for classification.
Explain that closer relatives have more similar DNA base sequences.
State the main features that place animals and plants in kingdoms.
State the features placing organisms in the five kingdoms: animal, plant, fungus, prokaryote, protoctist.
State the main features of vertebrate groups and arthropod groups.
Classify organisms using the features of animal groups.
State the features placing plants in ferns, dicotyledons and monocotyledons.
Classify organisms using the features of plant groups.
State the features of viruses: a protein coat and genetic material.
Describe and compare plant and animal cell structure.
Describe bacterial cell structure.
Identify these structures in diagrams and images.
Describe the functions of the structures.
State that new cells are produced by division of existing cells.
State the functions of specialised cells: ciliated, root hair, palisade, neurone, red blood and gametes.
Describe cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism.
State and use magnification = image size / actual size.
Calculate magnification and specimen size using millimetres.
Convert between millimetres and micrometres.

units.title: 3 Movement into and out of cells

outcomes.text: Describe diffusion as net movement down a concentration gradient due to random movement.
State that the energy for diffusion is kinetic energy of random molecular movement.
State that some substances cross the cell membrane by diffusion.
Describe the importance of diffusion of gases and solutes in organisms.
Investigate factors affecting diffusion: surface area, temperature, gradient and distance.
Describe water as a solvent in digestion, excretion and transport.
State that water diffuses through partially permeable membranes by osmosis and moves into and out of cells that way.
Describe osmosis as net movement of water from higher to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
Investigate osmosis using materials such as dialysis tubing.
Investigate the effects on plant tissues of solutions of different concentrations.
Explain these effects using turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis and flaccid.
State that water pressure in cells supports plants.
Explain the importance of water potential and osmosis in water uptake and loss.
Describe active transport as movement against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
State that protein carriers move molecules or ions across the membrane.
Explain its importance, including ion uptake by root hairs.
List the elements in carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
State that starch, glycogen and cellulose are made from glucose; proteins from amino acids; fats from fatty acids and glycerol.
Describe the iodine, Benedict's, biuret, ethanol emulsion and DCPIP tests.
Describe the DNA double helix of two coiled strands.
Describe bases on each strand and bonds between base pairs holding strands together.
State that A pairs with T and C with G.
Describe a catalyst as increasing reaction rate without being changed.
Describe enzymes as proteins that act as biological catalysts in all metabolic reactions.
Describe why enzymes matter: they give reaction rates needed to sustain life.
Describe enzyme action using the active site shape complementary to the substrate.
Explain action with active site, enzyme-substrate complex, substrate and product.
Explain enzyme specificity as complementary shape and fit.
Investigate the effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity, with optimum and denaturation.
Explain the temperature effect using kinetic energy, shape and fit, effective collisions and denaturation.
Explain the pH effect using shape and fit and denaturation.
Describe photosynthesis as plants making carbohydrates from raw materials using light energy.
State the word equation for photosynthesis.
State the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.
State that chlorophyll is a green pigment in chloroplasts that transfers light energy into chemical energy.
Outline uses of carbohydrates made: starch store, cellulose walls, glucose for respiration, sucrose transport and nectar.
Explain the importance of nitrate ions and magnesium ions.
Investigate the need for chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide using controls.
Investigate the effects of light intensity, carbon dioxide and temperature on rate.
Investigate light and dark effects on gas exchange in an aquatic plant using hydrogencarbonate indicator.
Identify and explain limiting factors of photosynthesis.
Explain how a large, thin leaf is adapted for photosynthesis.
Identify leaf structures in diagrams and images: cuticle, epidermis, mesophyll, guard cells, stomata, air spaces, vascular bundles.
Explain how these structures adapt leaves for photosynthesis.
Describe a balanced diet.
State dietary sources and importance of carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins C and D, calcium, iron, fibre and water.
State the causes of scurvy and rickets.
Identify the alimentary canal and associated organs in diagrams and images.
Describe the functions of these organs for ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion.
Describe physical digestion as breaking food into pieces without chemical change.
State that it increases surface area for enzymes.
Identify incisors, canines, premolars and molars.
Describe tooth structure: enamel, dentine, pulp, nerves, blood vessels and cement.
Describe the functions of the tooth types.
Describe the stomach's role in physical digestion.
Outline how bile emulsifies fats to increase surface area.
Describe chemical digestion as breaking large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones.
State its role in producing absorbable molecules.
Describe amylase, proteases and lipase and what they break down.
State where amylase, protease and lipase are secreted and act.

subtopics.title: Acid, bile and detail of digestion

outcomes.text: Describe hydrochloric acid in gastric juice: killing microorganisms and giving acidic pH.
Describe starch digestion by amylase to maltose and maltase to glucose.
Describe protein digestion by pepsin in the stomach and trypsin in the small intestine.
Explain bile as an alkaline mixture neutralising stomach acid for enzyme action.
State that nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
State that most water is absorbed in the small intestine and some in the colon.
Explain how villi and microvilli increase the internal surface area.
Describe the structure of a villus and the roles of capillaries and lacteals.
State that xylem transports water and mineral ions and supports; phloem transports sucrose and amino acids.
Identify xylem and phloem in sections of roots, stems and leaves of non-woody dicotyledons.
Relate xylem vessel structure to function: thick lignified walls, no contents, end-to-end cells with no cross walls.
Identify root hair cells and state their function.
State that the large root hair surface area increases water and mineral uptake.
Outline the water pathway: root hair, root cortex, xylem, mesophyll.
Investigate the pathway of water using a stain.
Describe transpiration as loss of water vapour from leaves.
State that water evaporates from mesophyll surfaces and diffuses out through stomata.
Explain how water loss relates to the internal air-space surface area and stomata size and number.
Explain how water rises in xylem by transpiration pull and attraction between water molecules.
Investigate the effects of temperature and wind speed on transpiration rate.
Explain the effects of temperature, wind speed and humidity on transpiration.
Explain how and why wilting occurs.
Describe translocation as movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks.
Describe sources as parts that release them and sinks as parts that use or store them.
Explain why a plant part may be a source and a sink at different times.
Describe the circulatory system: vessels, a pump and valves giving one-way flow.
Describe the single circulation of a fish.
Describe the double circulation of a mammal.
Explain the advantages of double circulation.
Identify mammalian heart structures: muscular wall, septum, ventricles, atria, one-way valves and coronary arteries.
Identify the atrioventricular and semilunar valves.
Explain the relative thickness of ventricle and atrial walls.
Explain the importance of the septum in separating oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
Describe how atria, ventricles and valves work together.
State that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it.
State how heart activity is monitored: ECG, pulse rate and valve sounds.
Investigate and explain the effect of physical activity on heart rate.
Describe coronary heart disease as blocked coronary arteries and state its risk factors.
Discuss the roles of diet and exercise in reducing coronary heart disease risk.
Describe artery, vein and capillary structure: wall thickness, lumen diameter, valves in veins.
State the functions of capillaries.
Explain how artery and vein structure relates to blood pressure.
Explain how capillary structure relates to function.
Identify the vena cava, aorta, pulmonary artery and vein, and renal artery and vein.
Identify the hepatic artery, hepatic veins and hepatic portal vein.
List the components of blood: red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
Identify red and white blood cells, lymphocytes and phagocytes in images.
State the functions of red cells (including haemoglobin), white cells, platelets and plasma.
State that lymphocytes make antibodies and phagocytes engulf pathogens.
State that clotting prevents blood loss and pathogen entry.
Describe clotting as fibrinogen converted to a fibrin mesh.
Describe a pathogen as a disease-causing organism.
Describe a transmissible disease as one whose pathogen passes between hosts.
State that pathogens are transmitted by direct contact or indirectly via surfaces, food, animals and air.
Describe body defences: skin, nose hairs, mucus, stomach acid and white blood cells.
Explain the importance of clean water, hygienic food preparation, personal hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment.
Describe active immunity as defence by antibody production.
State that each pathogen has antigens with specific shapes.
Describe antibodies as proteins binding antigens to destroy pathogens or mark them for phagocytes.
State that specific antibodies have shapes complementary to specific antigens.
Explain that active immunity follows infection or vaccination.
Outline vaccination: weakened pathogens or antigens, immune response, memory cells.
Explain the role of vaccination in controlling disease.
Explain passive immunity as short-term defence from another individual's antibodies, via placenta and breast milk.
Explain the importance of breast-feeding for passive immunity.
State that memory cells are not made in passive immunity.
Describe cholera as a bacterial disease transmitted in contaminated water.
Explain how the toxin causes chloride secretion, osmotic water movement, diarrhoea, dehydration and ion loss.

subtopics.title: Gas exchange surfaces and breathing system

outcomes.text: Describe gas exchange surface features: large area, thin, good blood supply and ventilation.
Identify the parts of the breathing system including alveoli and capillaries.
Identify internal and external intercostal muscles.
State the function of cartilage in the trachea.
Explain how ribs, intercostal muscles and diaphragm change thorax volume and pressure to ventilate the lungs.
Investigate air composition differences using limewater for carbon dioxide.
Describe the differences in oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Explain the differences in composition.
Investigate effects of physical activity on rate and depth of breathing.
Explain how raised blood carbon dioxide, detected by the brain, increases breathing rate and depth.
Explain how goblet cells, mucus and ciliated cells protect the breathing system.
State uses of energy: muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses and constant body temperature.
Investigate the effect of temperature on respiration in yeast.
Describe aerobic respiration as using oxygen to break down nutrients and release energy.
State the word equation for aerobic respiration.
State the balanced equation for aerobic respiration.
Describe anaerobic respiration as releasing energy without oxygen.
State that it releases much less energy per glucose than aerobic respiration.
State the equations for anaerobic respiration in yeast (word and balanced).
State the word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles.
State that lactic acid builds up in vigorous exercise, causing oxygen debt.
Outline removal of oxygen debt: continued fast heart rate, deeper breathing and aerobic breakdown of lactic acid in the liver.
State that carbon dioxide is excreted through the lungs.
State that the kidneys excrete urea, excess water and ions.
Identify kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra, and kidney cortex and medulla in images.
Outline the nephron: glomerular filtration of water, glucose, urea and ions.
Outline reabsorption of all glucose, some ions and most water.
Outline formation of urine with urea, excess water and ions.
Describe the liver's role in assimilating amino acids into proteins.
State that urea forms in the liver from excess amino acids.
Describe deamination.
Explain the importance of excretion: toxicity of urea.
State that electrical impulses travel along neurones.
Describe the central and peripheral nervous systems.
Describe the nervous system's role in coordination and regulation.
Identify sensory, relay and motor neurones.
Describe a simple reflex arc: receptor, sensory, relay and motor neurone, effector.
Describe a reflex action as automatic and rapid coordination of stimuli with effector responses.
Describe a synapse as a junction between two neurones.
Describe synapse structure: vesicles of neurotransmitter, gap and receptor proteins.
Describe events at a synapse: release, diffusion, binding and a new impulse.
State that synapses ensure one-way impulses.
Describe sense organs as receptor groups responding to specific stimuli.
Identify eye structures: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve and blind spot.
Describe the function of each eye part.
Explain the pupil reflex with light intensity and pupil diameter.
Explain the pupil reflex through antagonistic circular and radial iris muscles.
Explain accommodation: ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments, lens shape and refraction.
Describe the distribution of rods and cones in the retina.
Outline rods for night vision and three cone types for colour.
Identify the fovea and state its function.
Describe a hormone as a chemical from a gland, carried in blood, altering target organs.
Identify adrenal glands, pancreas, testes and ovaries and the hormones they secrete.
State that glucagon is secreted by the pancreas.
Describe adrenaline in fight or flight: breathing rate, heart rate and pupil diameter.
Describe adrenaline raising blood glucose and heart rate in metabolic control.
Compare nervous and hormonal control by speed and duration.
Describe homeostasis as maintaining a constant internal environment.
Explain negative feedback with a set point.
State that insulin decreases blood glucose.
Describe blood glucose control by the liver, insulin and glucagon.
Outline the treatment of Type 1 diabetes.
Identify skin structures: hairs, erector muscles, sweat glands, receptors, neurones, blood vessels, fatty tissue.
Describe temperature control by insulation, sweating, shivering and the brain.
Describe temperature control by vasodilation and vasoconstriction of skin arterioles.
Describe gravitropism as growth towards or away from gravity.
Describe phototropism as growth towards or away from light.
Investigate gravitropism and phototropism in shoots and roots.
Explain phototropism and gravitropism as chemical control of growth.
Explain auxin: made in the shoot tip, diffuses, unevenly distributed by light and gravity, stimulates cell elongation.
Describe a drug as a substance that modifies chemical reactions in the body.
Describe antibiotics for bacterial infections.
State that antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses.
State that resistant bacteria reduce antibiotic effectiveness.
Explain how using antibiotics only when essential limits resistance such as MRSA.
Describe asexual reproduction as one parent producing genetically identical offspring.
Identify examples of asexual reproduction.
Discuss advantages and disadvantages for wild populations and for crop production.
Describe sexual reproduction as fusion of two gametes' nuclei, giving genetically different offspring.
Describe fertilisation as fusion of gamete nuclei.
State that gametes are haploid and the zygote is diploid.
Discuss advantages and disadvantages for wild populations and for crop production.
Identify and draw the parts of an insect-pollinated flower.
State the functions of these parts.
Identify and describe anthers and stigmas of a wind-pollinated flower.
Distinguish insect-pollinated from wind-pollinated pollen grains.
Describe pollination.
Describe structural adaptations of insect- and wind-pollinated flowers.
Describe self-pollination.
Describe cross-pollination.
Discuss effects of each on variation, response to change and reliance on pollinators.
State that fertilisation occurs when pollen nucleus fuses with an ovule nucleus.
Describe pollen tube growth, entry into the ovule and fertilisation.
Investigate conditions for germination: water, oxygen and suitable temperature.
Identify and state functions of the male reproductive parts.
Identify and state functions of the female reproductive parts.
Describe fertilisation as fusion of sperm and egg nuclei.
Explain adaptive features of sperm.
Explain adaptive features of egg cells.
Compare male and female gametes in size, structure, motility and numbers.
State that the zygote forms an embryo that implants in the uterus lining.
Identify and state functions of the umbilical cord, placenta, amniotic sac and fluid.
Describe the placenta and cord exchanging nutrients, gases and wastes.
State that some pathogens and toxins cross the placenta.
Describe testosterone and oestrogen in puberty and secondary sexual characteristics.
Describe the menstrual cycle through ovary and uterus lining changes.
Describe where oestrogen and progesterone are produced in the cycle and pregnancy.
Explain how FSH, LH, progesterone and oestrogen control the cycle and pregnancy.
Describe an STI as an infection spread by sexual contact.
State that HIV is a pathogen causing an STI and may lead to AIDS.
Describe HIV transmission.
Explain how STI spread is controlled.
State that chromosomes are DNA containing genes.
Define a gene as a length of DNA coding for a protein.
Define an allele as an alternative form of a gene.
Describe sex inheritance with X and Y chromosomes.
State that base sequence in a gene determines amino acid sequence.
Explain that different amino acid sequences give different protein shapes.
Explain that DNA controls cell function by controlling production of proteins, including enzymes, carriers and receptors.
Explain how a protein is made: gene stays in the nucleus, mRNA copies it, moves to cytoplasm, ribosome assembles amino acids in the sequence set by mRNA bases.
Explain that most body cells have the same genes but express only the ones for the proteins they need.
Describe a haploid nucleus as having a single set of chromosomes.
Describe a diploid nucleus as having two sets.
State that diploid cells have chromosome pairs, with 23 pairs in humans.
Describe mitosis as nuclear division producing genetically identical cells.
State the role of mitosis in growth, repair, replacement and asexual reproduction.
State that chromosomes replicate exactly before mitosis.
State that chromosome copies separate in mitosis, keeping chromosome number in daughter cells.
Describe stem cells as unspecialised cells dividing by mitosis that can become specialised.
State that meiosis produces gametes.
Describe meiosis as reduction division halving chromosome number from diploid to haploid, giving genetically different cells.
Describe inheritance as passing genetic information between generations.
Describe genotype as genetic make-up and phenotype as observable features.
Describe homozygous and heterozygous, and which are pure-breeding.
Describe dominant and recessive alleles.
Interpret pedigree diagrams.
Use genetic diagrams to predict monohybrid crosses with 1:1 and 3:1 ratios.
Use Punnett squares to show possible genotypes.
Explain how a test cross identifies an unknown genotype.
Describe codominance.
Explain inheritance of ABO blood groups with alleles IA, IB and Io.
Describe sex-linked characteristics and why they are more common in one sex.
Describe red-green colour blindness as sex linkage.
Predict crosses involving codominance or sex linkage.
Describe variation as differences between individuals of one species.
State that continuous variation gives a range of phenotypes between extremes.
State that discontinuous variation gives a limited number of phenotypes without intermediates.
State that discontinuous variation is caused by genes only; continuous by genes and environment.
Investigate examples of continuous and discontinuous variation.
Describe mutation as genetic change and the source of new alleles.
State that ionising radiation and some chemicals raise the mutation rate.
Describe gene mutation as a random change in DNA base sequence.
State that mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation give variation.
Describe an adaptive feature as an inherited feature that helps survival and reproduction.
Interpret information about a species to describe its adaptive features.
Explain the adaptive features of hydrophytes and xerophytes.
Describe natural selection: variation, many offspring, struggle for survival, better-adapted individuals reproduce more, alleles passed on.
Describe adaptation as populations becoming better suited over generations.
Describe antibiotic-resistant bacteria as an example of natural selection.
Describe selective breeding: humans select, cross, and select offspring with desirable features.
Outline selective breeding over generations to improve crops and animals.
Outline differences between natural and artificial selection.
State that the Sun is the main energy source for biological systems.
Describe energy flow from sunlight to chemical energy in organisms and eventually to the environment.
Describe a food chain as energy transfer starting with a producer.
Construct and interpret simple food chains.
Describe a food web as interconnected chains and interpret food webs.
Use food chains and webs to describe human impact through overharvesting and introduced species.
Describe a producer.
Describe a consumer and classify primary to quaternary consumers.
Describe herbivores and carnivores.
Describe a decomposer.
Describe a trophic level and identify trophic levels in food webs and pyramids.
Draw, describe and interpret pyramids of numbers and biomass.
Discuss advantages of biomass pyramids over numbers.
Draw and interpret pyramids of energy and discuss their advantages.
Explain why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient.
Explain why food chains usually have fewer than five trophic levels.
Explain why eating crops is more energy efficient than eating livestock fed on crops.
Describe the carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossil fuel formation and combustion.
Describe the nitrogen cycle: decomposition to ammonium, nitrification, nitrogen fixation, nitrate absorption, amino acid and protein production, feeding, deamination and denitrification.
State the roles of microorganisms in the nitrogen cycle.
Describe a population.
Describe a community.
Describe an ecosystem.
State factors affecting population growth: food supply, competition, predation and disease.
Identify the lag, exponential, stationary and death phases of the sigmoid curve.
Interpret graphs and diagrams of population growth.
Explain the factors behind each phase, including limiting factors.
Describe how humans raise food production: machinery, fertilisers, insecticides, herbicides and selective breeding.
Describe advantages and disadvantages of large-scale monocultures.
Describe advantages and disadvantages of intensive livestock production.
Describe biodiversity as the number of species in an area.
Describe reasons for habitat destruction: housing, farming, resource extraction and pollution.
State that altering food webs can harm habitats.
Explain the effects of deforestation: lost biodiversity, extinction, soil loss, flooding and more carbon dioxide.
Describe the effects of untreated sewage and excess fertiliser on aquatic ecosystems.
Explain eutrophication: more nitrate, producer growth, decomposition, decomposer respiration, less oxygen, death of organisms.
Describe the effects of non-biodegradable plastics.
Describe sources and effects of methane and carbon dioxide pollution: enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change.
Describe a sustainable resource.
State that forests and fish stocks can be conserved and managed sustainably.
Explain forest conservation: education, protected areas, quotas and replanting.
Explain fish stock conservation: education, closed seasons, protected areas, nets, quotas and monitoring.
Explain why organisms become endangered or extinct.
Describe how endangered species are conserved: monitoring, education, captive breeding and seed banks.
Describe reasons for conservation programmes.
Describe AI and IVF in captive breeding.
Explain the risks to a species of reduced genetic variation.
State that bacteria are useful because they reproduce rapidly and make complex molecules.
Discuss why bacteria suit biotechnology: few ethical concerns and plasmids.
Describe anaerobic respiration in yeast making ethanol for biofuels.
Describe anaerobic respiration in yeast in bread-making.
Describe pectinase in fruit juice production.
Investigate biological washing powders containing enzymes.
Explain lactase producing lactose-free milk.
Describe fermenters for large-scale production of insulin, penicillin and mycoprotein.
Describe and explain fermenter conditions: temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrients and waste.
Describe genetic modification as changing an organism's genetic material by removing, changing or inserting genes.
Outline examples: human genes in bacteria, and crop genes for herbicide resistance, pest resistance and nutrition.

subtopics.title: Making a human protein in bacteria

outcomes.text: Outline isolating a human gene with restriction enzymes forming sticky ends.
Outline cutting bacterial plasmid with the same enzymes.
Outline inserting the gene with DNA ligase to make a recombinant plasmid.
Outline inserting plasmids into bacteria, multiplying them and expressing the human protein.
Discuss advantages and disadvantages of genetically modifying crops such as soya, maize and rice.
